title: Electrostriction in a Bose-Einstein Condensate of Dipolar Molecules
authors: Haneul Kwak, Ian Stevenson, Weijun Yuan, Siwei Zhang, Asaf Toprakci, Lin Su, Tijs Karman, Sebastian Will
abstract: The recent creation of a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) of dipolar molecules has opened a new frontier for many-body quantum systems in which dipolar interactions can drive novel self-organization phenomena. Here, we observe electrostriction in a molecular BEC, an elliptical deformation driven by anisotropic dipolar interactions. We use double microwave dressing, involving $σ$- and $π$-polarized fields, to control non-axially symmetric dipolar interactions. We compare the experimental observations of electrostriction to a model based on an extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation and find excellent agreement in the regime of weak to moderate interactions. Using electrostriction, we demonstrate that the molecular BEC can be torqued by dynamically changing the orientation of the elliptical $σ$ microwave field. This provides a route to setting molecular quantum gases into rotation, opening opportunities to probe vorticity, superfluidity, and supersolidity in strongly dipolar matter.
summary: This study investigates electrostriction in a BEC of dipolar molecules, using microwave dressing to precisely control the anisotropic dipole-dipole interactions. By modeling the system with an extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation, the authors confirm the theoretical predictions against experimental measurements of cloud deformation. Crucially, they demonstrate that this control mechanism can be used to torque the BEC, providing a novel tool to probe fundamental quantum phenomena like superfluidity and vorticity in dipolar quantum gases.
main_problem: The study focuses on observing and modeling electrostriction—an elliptical deformation—in a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC) of dipolar molecules, and demonstrating the ability to torque the BEC by controlling the dipole-dipole interaction orientation.
main_result: Electrostriction was successfully observed and modeled with excellent agreement using an extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation (eGPE). Furthermore, the anisotropic dipolar interactions allow for dynamically torquing the BEC, opening pathways to study vorticity and superfluidity.
method: The research combines experimental measurements (time-of-flight expansion, cloud shape analysis) with theoretical modeling using the extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation (eGPE) incorporating Lee-Huang-Yang (LHY) corrections.
model_or_system: The system is a BEC of dipolar molecules (e.g., NaCs) trapped in an external potential. The dynamics are governed by an eGPE that includes both short-range contact interactions and long-range, anisotropic dipolar interactions, which are tuned via double microwave dressing.
key_observables: Cloud shape, aspect ratio, electrostriction magnitude, and the resulting torque/rotation of the condensate.
important_parameters: Ellipticity ($\xi$) and orientation ($\phi$) of the microwave dressing field; dipolar lengths ($a_d$); interaction regimes (weak to moderate interactions).
main_assumptions: The model relies on the eGPE framework, which approximates the short-range potential as a contact interaction, and the LHY term is used to account for beyond-mean-field quantum fluctuations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the anisotropic expansion of the BEC during time-of-flight, showing the dependence of cloud size on the microwave dressing ellipticity ($\xi$), and demonstrating the torque induced by changing the microwave polarization.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical phenomenon (electrostriction) using microwave dressing to control dipolar interactions. It then models the dynamics using the eGPE, comparing theory to experimental measurements of cloud expansion. Finally, it utilizes this control to induce rotation, opening avenues for studying superfluid properties.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controllable platform to study many-body quantum dynamics in dipolar systems, moving beyond simple mean-field descriptions by incorporating LHY corrections and demonstrating active control over macroscopic quantum properties like rotation and vorticity.
